structured_output.hypothesis: Height-velocity curves for boys and girls aged about 5 to 19 have nearly the same shape once one is shifted in age, and the girls' adolescent acceleration begins, peaks and ends earlier than the boys', with a somewhat different peak amplitude.
structured_output.pass_criterion: From the WHO 2007 median height-for-age by month (LMS median M), compute annual velocity (cm/yr) for each sex, smoothed over 12 months. All three conditions must hold. (1) Girls' peak-velocity age is earlier than boys' by at least 1.0 year. (2) Girls' take-off age, defined as the age after the pre-pubertal minimum at which velocity first exceeds the minimum by 1 cm/yr, and girls' end age, defined as the age after the peak at which velocity falls below 2 cm/yr, are both earlier than the boys' counterparts. (3) After shifting the girls' curve in age by the best-fit lag, the Pearson correlation between the sexes over ages 8 to 17 is at least 0.90. The peak amplitudes must also differ by at least 5% in relative terms, which is the stated amplitude difference.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if any one of these holds. The girls' peak age precedes the boys' by less than 0.5 year, or does not precede it at all. The girls' take-off or end age is not earlier than the boys'. The best-lag correlation of the two velocity curves is below 0.80, meaning the shapes are not similar. Intermediate results (phase difference 0.5 to 1.0 year, or correlation 0.80 to 0.90) count as inconclusive, not as a pass.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'curve of growth velocity' is the first derivative of stature with age, so it is measured as cm per year. 'Phase' means the age of onset, peak and end of the adolescent acceleration, and 'amplitude' means peak velocity. 'Similar shape' is operationalised as the correlation of the velocity curves after an age shift. Modern reinterpretation: the WHO reference gives smoothed cross-sectional population medians, not individual longitudinal growth. Velocity derived from it is therefore a population-median velocity and will blur individual peak height velocity, which understates peak amplitude. The phase comparison between the sexes should still be valid. Thompson's own data were longitudinal series (Bowditch, Quetelet, Godin).

dataset.name: Growth reference data for 5-19 years (WHO 2007)
dataset.why_it_fits: It provides downloadable tables of height-for-age by sex, by month from 61 to 228 months, with L, M and S values and percentiles. The M (median) column for boys and girls gives the stature curves, and differencing them gives velocity curves for the phase, amplitude and shape comparison. It is public, measured rather than self-reported, and sex-specific.
